surSpeed:
35.6 ms per flush with the physics model, 7.3 µs with the network: about 4,894 times faster.

Both timings are measured in this browser. A high-fidelity run of a flush, SPH or VOF, takes minutes to hours, so a network trained on such runs could be faster still by a much larger factor. That is a rough expectation, not a benchmark, and the training runs would have to be paid for first.

hybSum:
Mean error on unseen designs, cleaned and solids removed, in percentage points: uncalibrated 9.4 / 7.0, calibrated 4.9 / 2.3, hybrid 4.9 / 2.0.

Calibration removes most of the error; the correction takes off a little more.

Fitted coefficients need not match the hidden values exactly: several coefficient sets can explain the same few runs, and the hidden effects push the fit away from them. That is why the hold-out error, not the coefficient match, is the test.

nzSum:
How well the model matches the measured differences between designs, root mean square in dB: current coefficients 0.52, fitted 0.17. On designs left out of the fit one at a time: current 0.63, fitted 0.23.

The fit improves the prediction for designs it did not see, so the fitted coefficients carry over.

Recordings can only show what differs between the designs. A coefficient that changes all designs alike, or none of them, cannot be fitted from them and stays close to its current value. The hidden reference adds a valve click, fill valve noise and a low-pitched gurgle the model does not know about, so the fitted values need not equal the hidden ones; what counts is the error on designs left out. The gurgle, for example, is low-pitched, so A-weighting takes about 7 dB off it, and the fit lowers the trap weight to match: that is what a calibration against real recordings should do too.

pnDense:
From 81 noisy readings, the network found a weir coefficient of 1.44; the hidden value is 1.45 (−1 %). The model's default of 1.7 would have been 17 % off.

It also estimates what was never measured: about 0.8 L of water on the wall at 1 s; the full model holds 0.95 L there.

Honest comparison: classic least squares, which integrates the same equation for trial values, finds 1.50 (+4 %) in 34 ms; the network takes 2.0 s. For a small equation like this one, the classic fit is the better tool. PINNs pay off when the equations are expensive to solve over and over, partly unknown, or the data are scattered in space and time. For a full three-dimensional flush with turbulence and free surfaces, CFD plus surrogate models is the realistic route. Both fits differ from 1.45 by a few percent because the simple pool equation does not capture every detail of the full model's wall flow.

fsSum:
Trained on 80 expensive runs, about 27 virtual days of CFD, the pure data surrogate matches the cleaned area of unseen designs to 84 % and misses the cleaned share by 9.6 points. The fast physics model, with no expensive runs at all: 95 % and 1.7 points. With a learned correction of its map: 95 % and 1.6 points.

The data surrogate is the quickest to ask, about 115 µs for a whole map against 56 ms for the fast model, and it gets better with more runs, slowly (80 % with 10 runs). But it has to learn the physics from examples, and here even 80 runs are not enough to catch up with a model built on the same equations as the reference.

Read this with care: the reference maps come from the same flush model with other coefficients (the extra effects of the challenge's reference change its totals, not its maps). That gives the fast model a head start it would not have against real CFD, and it is also why the correction adds little: the maps differ mostly in level, not in pattern. The CFD check shows real pattern differences (streaks behind the jets, the pool washing the wall near the waterline); against real CFD runs, a learned map correction would have more to learn. Field surrogates such as SimAI, Simcenter PhysicsAI or PhysicsNeMo are trained on hundreds of CFD runs; they pay off when there is no fast physics model, or when every design study reuses the same run database.
